population_age: as_reported: 18–29 years | maps_10_19: False | maps_10_24: True | maps_18_24: True
languages_supported: The study was conducted in English and isiZulu. Participants completed IDIs and FGDs in their preferred language (English or isiZulu). All interviews and FGDs were completed by experienced, trained interviewers proficient in both English and isiZulu. The chatbot itself appears to have operated primarily in English via Telegram. Multilingual capabilities were deemed essential, particularly for users more comfortable expressing themselves in local languages like isiZulu. Participants suggested that sometimes it becomes difficult to express what you want to say in English, and that the chatbot should understand and operate in multiple local languages. No formal translation/localization process for the chatbot is described.
device_connectivity: The chatbot was accessed via the Telegram mobile app interfacing with the OpenAI gpt-4-turbo model. During the study, participants used a study-provided laptop. High data costs were identified as a major barrier, with participants noting that data consumption was a significant concern and emphasizing the need for data-free usage and multiplatform access, especially via widely used apps like WhatsApp. All participants reported prior use of social media platforms, suggesting general familiarity with digital technologies. No offline/low-data functionality, shared-device use, or electricity constraints were described.
cultural_adaptation: The chatbot was developed to provide an introductory module of the Inuka coaching training program, which is an online problem-solving therapy training program based on the evidence-based Friendship Bench program originally developed in Zimbabwe. The chatbot was trained using anonymous transcripts from previous Inuka in-person online coaching sessions. A coordinating agent applied an appropriate stylistic tone tailored to the target population. The IDI guides were developed by reviewing current literature and engaging in discussions with the research team, local community partners, thematic experts and young people. No formal adaptation framework (e.g., Bernal) is named. Participants viewed the chatbot as culturally relevant but recommended multilingual capabilities and culturally sensitive improvements.
implementation_contexts: The study was conducted at the Aurum POP INN clinic in Pietermaritzburg, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, within an HIV prevention/treatment service context. The chatbot was offered to MSM and TGW using HIV prevention or treatment programs as part of a broader mental health well-being initiative. The setting is a key-population-friendly clinic in a high HIV burden district (antenatal HIV prevalence 40.7%). Implementation stage: pilot/feasibility qualitative study. There are limited options available for members of the LGBTQI+ community to access services focused on their health needs, and where available, they are concentrated in urban centres, making access difficult for those in outlying areas.
sa_language_coverage: Interviews conducted in English or isiZulu. Multilingual capabilities deemed essential, with participants requesting isiZulu and isiXhosa support. Code-switching difficulties noted when expressing emotions in English vs local languages.
